section_summary: This section contains correspondence, memoranda, telegrams, and cross-reference sheets (1930–1936) regarding persistent proposals by United Press journalist Henry F. Misselwitz to organize professional baseball in Japan and inaugurate an international World Series between American and Japanese champions. Misselwitz repeatedly lobbied Secretaries of State Henry L. Stimson and Cordell Hull, as well as White House Assistant Secretary Stephen T. Early, seeking official or informal administration endorsement to aid his promotional efforts and foster Japanese-American goodwill. The Department of State consistently declined to provide official backing or authorize the public use of officials' names, maintaining an established policy against connecting the government with private commercial enterprises while affirming informal sympathy for athletic exchanges.

subfiles.about: A personal letter from Henry F. Misselwitz congratulating Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson on the London Naval Conference and requesting a weekend meeting in Washington.
subfiles.summary: United Press's Henry Misselwitz plans a weekend visit to Washington, asks to meet Stimson, congratulates him on the London Naval Conference, and requests a reply to confirm.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter from Secretary Stimson regretting that he cannot meet with Misselwitz due to the visit of the President-elect of Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Stimson replies to Misselwitz's June 4 letter that he can't see him the next two weekends because of the Brazilian President-elect Prestes's visit, and suggests postponing.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter from Misselwitz agreeing to postpone his Washington visit and requesting a luncheon appointment on June 21.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz thanks Stimson, postpones his trip a week, and asks to schedule a luncheon on Saturday, June 21, 1930.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter from Secretary Stimson explaining that he will be out of town on June 21 and offering only a brief midweek appointment.
subfiles.summary: Stimson says he will be away Saturday, June 21, because post-London Conference work limits engagements, but might see Misselwitz briefly mid-week.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum analyzing Henry F. Misselwitz's proposal to organize baseball in Japan and establish a World Series.
subfiles.summary: Ransford Miller summarizes Misselwitz's proposal to organize baseball in Japan with an international World Series, using only Japanese capital; Miller doubts professional baseball can avoid commercialization or that capital is available, favoring collegiate exchanges.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Ransford S. Miller on Misselwitz's Proposal to Organize Baseball in Japan

subfiles.about: An archival document withdrawal sheet inserted into the file jacket.
subfiles.summary: Archival document withdrawal sheet, faint and largely unreadable; the removed item can't be identified.
subfiles.title: Document Withdrawal Sheet

subfiles.about: A memorandum forwarding Henry F. Misselwitz's letter to Dr. Hornbeck for advice and a draft reply.
subfiles.summary: E.R.M. sends Misselwitz's letter to Hornbeck, noting he's a friend of Stimson, who hasn't seen the proposal, and asks a memorandum or draft reply with Hornbeck's opinion.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from E. R. M. to Stanley K. Hornbeck

subfiles.about: A confidential letter proposing the organization of professional baseball in Japan and an international World Series to foster friendship.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz confidentially proposes organizing professional baseball in Japan and an international World Series, citing 75,000 spectators at high school championships and Dr. Isoo Abe's collegiate roots; he seeks Stimson's advice and unofficial support and hopes to be American advisor.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter from Secretary Stimson expressing sympathy with the goal of international sports friendship but questioning the practicability of commercial baseball in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Stimson confidentially replies to Misselwitz's October 2 letter that he sympathizes with good Japan-U.S. relations but doubts the plan, questioning how baseball could avoid commercialization or find Japanese capital, and suggests sounding out Japanese friends.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A telegram thanking Secretary Stimson for his letter and requesting an appointment in Washington on Saturday.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz telegraphs thanks for Stimson's letter, plans to come to Washington Saturday morning to see him, and asks if convenient.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A telegraphic reply from Secretary Stimson declining a weekend meeting due to his absence from Washington.
subfiles.summary: Stimson telegraphs Misselwitz he leaves Washington Friday noon and returns Monday afternoon, so no Saturday meeting is possible.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter outlining a detailed plan to seek support from organized baseball and requesting State Department letters of endorsement and introduction.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz asks Stimson for an informal letter favoring the Japanese baseball project and an introduction to Ambassador Forbes, argues business methods support a Pacific-understanding ideal, and plans to approach Commissioner Landis and William Wrigley Jr.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter declining official support for commercialized sports promotion but providing a general letter of introduction to diplomatic officers.
subfiles.summary: Stimson, replying to the October 15 letter, sympathizes with friendly relations but declines official support for a commercialized plan, which must proceed privately, and encloses a general letter of introduction usable with Ambassador Forbes.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter reporting progress with baseball authorities and inquiring whether Stimson's letter may be used in press announcements in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz reports Commissioner Landis and league presidents Heydler and Barnard are submitting the Japanese baseball proposal to club owners, a tour of American players to Japan was approved, and he asks to use Stimson's October 18, 1930 letter in Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter prohibiting the public or press use of Department correspondence in connection with a private enterprise.
subfiles.summary: Stimson asks Misselwitz not to use his October 18, 1930 letter in public or press announcements in Japan, since using official correspondence for private enterprise violates Department policy; he congratulates him on progress.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A telegram inquiring whether Secretary Stimson had received his letter of January 7.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz telegraphs Stimson asking whether his letter of January 7, 1931 was received.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A telegraphic reply confirming that Misselwitz's letter was received and a response mailed.
subfiles.summary: Stimson telegraphs Misselwitz in New York that his letter was received and an official written reply was mailed that day.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording an invitation for the Harvard University baseball team to play in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Harvard's president's December 27, 1933 letter proposing a baseball team visit to Japan, with an invitation from Japanese universities, file 032 Harvard Ball Team/1.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Visit of Harvard University Ball Team to Japan

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording an inquiry regarding Harvard baseball games in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: William Bingham's May 18, 1934 telegram on Harvard baseball matches against Japanese universities and whether colleges sponsor them, file 032 Harvard Ball Team/3.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Harvard Baseball Team Tour in Japan

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum advising against supporting a professional baseball league in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs recommends against encouraging Misselwitz's renewed request for support of a Japanese major baseball league, noting Japan shows little interest in professional baseball and past international games often harmed relations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on Proposed Professional Baseball League in Japan

subfiles.about: A letter asking for an informal letter from Secretary Hull or an introduction to Ambassador Grew for his baseball venture.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz tells McDermott formal government action is inappropriate but an informal note from Hull or an introduction to Ambassador Grew would help, cites his Stimson correspondence and Japan's baseball enthusiasm, and asks confidentiality.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Michael J. McDermott

subfiles.about: A letter enclosing Misselwitz's reply to McDermott and requesting that President Roosevelt be informed of the baseball project.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz sends Stephen Early his reply to McDermott, hopes for an informal State note to enlist Judge Landis while keeping government uncommitted, and offers to tell Roosevelt in person.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Stephen T. Early

subfiles.about: A White House letter referring Henry F. Misselwitz's baseball proposal to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Early sends McDermott Misselwitz's confidential letter, calls the Japanese baseball project interesting but not for White House action, and asks State to reply confidentially for both offices.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stephen T. Early to Michael J. McDermott

subfiles.about: A detailed proposal to the White House advocating the organization of the National League of Japan to improve diplomatic relations.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz confidentially proposes a National League of Japan, calling baseball a "New Deal" diplomatic tool leading to an international World Series, citing fan passion, Babe Ruth and school tournaments, and asks informal encouragement and introductions.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Stephen T. Early

subfiles.about: A memorandum recommending an informal White House reply to Misselwitz and enclosing a draft letter.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck advises McDermott that Early should reply to Misselwitz directly to keep confidentiality, enclosing a draft: neither White House nor State can officially back a private venture, but officials like Grew will give informal courtesies such as throwing out the first ball.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Michael J. McDermott with Enclosed Draft Letter to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter informing Misselwitz that the administration cannot officially endorse a private commercial enterprise.
subfiles.summary: McDermott tells Misselwitz the administration can't officially back his Japanese baseball scheme, since private ventures would bring endless demands and discrimination charges, but officials will watch sympathetically and Grew will give informal courtesies like the first pitch.
subfiles.title: Letter from Michael J. McDermott to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A memorandum providing a suggested draft reply to Misselwitz regarding a proposed letter of introduction.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs submits a draft reply to Misselwitz's September 21, 1934 letter, noting introductions need clearance, restating the government can't join a private venture, and offering a general letter of introduction and sending the correspondence to Grew.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs to Michael J. McDermott with Enclosed Draft Reply to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter following up on an in-person meeting with Secretary Hull regarding the National League of Japan, enclosing a suggested endorsement letter.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull following a personal conference in Hull's office regarding the establishment of the National League of Japan. Misselwitz claims that President Roosevelt and Japanese Ambassador Hirosi Saito privately expressed enthusiastic support for the initiative and envisioned an international World Series with games in New York, Washington, Japan, and Honolulu. He requests an informal expression of sympathy from Hull to help him obtain written backing from Commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis, enclosing a pre-drafted letter of endorsement for the Secretary's signature.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Cordell Hull with Enclosed Suggested Reply

subfiles.about: A letter on behalf of Secretary Hull declining to authorize the use of the Secretary's name in support of a private enterprise.
subfiles.summary: Harry McBride tells Misselwitz that Hull, after consideration, sees no reason to change Stimson's 1931 and McDermott's 1934 views and doesn't feel warranted authorizing his name for a private commercial enterprise.
subfiles.title: Letter from Harry A. McBride to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter expressing regret over Secretary Hull's decision while thanking the Department for its informal interest.
subfiles.summary: Misselwitz regrets Hull, like Stimson, treats his National League of Japan project as private enterprise rather than a harbinger of Pacific goodwill, but thanks him for personal interest and off-the-record good wishes.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Harry A. McBride
